Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.
  • Kubernetes patch versions 1.36.3, 1.35.7, and 1.34.10 are available.
  • On-Demand Monitor for node health checks is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026: - Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools. - AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools. - Existing node pools won’t receive security patches. On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options: - Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade. - Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools. For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Ubuntu 20.04 has been replaced by newer supported versions, including Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04. We encourage you to transition to Ubuntu 22.04+ before the retirement date. Required action: If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with a Confidential VM (CVM) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.33+ where Ubuntu 24.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for CVM workloads. If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with Federal Information Process Standard (FIPS) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ where Ubuntu 22.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for FIPS workloads. To avoid service disruptions, scaling restrictions, and remain supported, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ by March 17, 2027. On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity. We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup. We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service. If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

On June 30, 2027, we'll retire Ubuntu 22.04 on Azure Kubernetes Service. To avoid disruptions, transition to Ubuntu 24.04 or later by that date. Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements. Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Migration Options: - Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later. - Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Read moreRead less
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters: - Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase) - Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready) After this change: - Metric names remain unchanged. - Aggregate pod counts remain available. - Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported. - The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting. During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement. You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow: - Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension. - Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension. Recommended action: - If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required. - If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics. Help and support If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Read moreRead less
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027. Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster. After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Read moreRead less
Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation. How does this affect me? - Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry. - Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028. - Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028. Required Action Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started. Signing: - Use AKV with self-signed certificates - Use AKV with CA-issued certificates - Sign in ADO pipelines - Sign in GitHub workflows Verification: - Verify in ADO pipelines - Verify in GitHub workflows - Verify on AKS

Read moreRead less
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date. Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements. From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date. On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail. Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions: - If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+. - Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here. To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

Its `istio-proxy` container in `applink-system` requires the following settings:++| Setting | Why ztunnel needs it |+| --- | --- |+| `runAsUser: 0`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: true` | The proxy runs as root and enters workload network namespaces. By default, NAP node pool virtual machines (VMs) are automatically updated when a new image version is available. You can configure an AKS-managed node operating system (OS) upgrade schedule maintenance window to control when new images are picked up and applied to your NAP nodes, or use Karpenter Node Disruption Budgets and Pod Disruption Budgets to control how and when disruption occurs during upgrades. +When you omit `spec.versions`, nodes use the observed AKS control-plane Kubernetes version, and the provider automatically resolves compatible node images. When the provider detects a control-plane Kubernetes version upgrade, it marks node images as not ready and resolves images for that Kubernetes version. The provider doesn't currently automatically downgrade node Kubernetes versions.++### Pin node image and Kubernetes version++NAP supports pinning the latest node image version and supported Kubernetes versions for NAP-managed nodes via the `spec.versions` field in the `AKSNodeClass` custom resource. The latest node image version can be pinned until its Kubernetes version is no longer supported (or not in Long-Term Support). When a pinned node image's Kubernetes version is no longer supported, the node image automatically updates to the next available supported node image version.++To pin Kubernetes or node image versions in NAP, see [Configure `AKSNodeClass` version settings](node-auto-provisioning-aksnodeclass#kubernetes-and-node-image-versions).+ ## Node OS upgrade maintenance windows for NAP -You can use the [AKS planned maintenance feature](planned-maintenance) with a [node OS auto-upgrade channel](auto-upgrade-node-os-image) to configure a `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule` maintenance window that controls when to perform node OS security patching scheduled by your designated node OS auto-upgrade channel.+Use the [AKS planned maintenance feature](planned-maintenance) with a [node OS auto-upgrade channel](auto-upgrade-node-os-image) to configure an `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule` maintenance window. This window controls when to perform node OS security patching scheduled by your designated node OS auto-upgrade channel.  ### Node OS upgrade maintenance window behavior and considerations  Keep the following information in mind when configuring a node OS upgrade maintenance window for NAP: -- The `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule` maintenance configuration determines the window during which NAP picks up a new image. This configuration doesn't necessarily determine when existing nodes are disrupted.-- The upgrade mechanism and decision criteria are specific to NAP/Karpenter and are evaluated by NAP's drift logic. NAP respects Karpenter Node Disruption Budgets and Pod Disruption Budgets. For more information about drift, see the [Karpenter drift documentation](https://karpenter.sh/docs/concepts/disruption/#drift).-- These NAP upgrade decisions are separate from the cluster `NodeImage` and `SecurityPatch` channels. However, the `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule` maintenance configuration applies them as well.+- The `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule` maintenance window gates routine automatic node image roll-forward. This configuration doesn't necessarily determine when existing nodes are disrupted.+- The upgrade mechanism and decision criteria are specific to NAP/Karpenter and are evaluated by NAP's drift logic. NAP respects Karpenter Node Disruption Budgets and Pod Disruption Budgets. For more information about drift, see the [NAP Drift documentation](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#drift).+- The maintenance window doesn't defer required image initialization, image pin changes or removal, or image refreshes associated with Kubernetes version changes.+- These NAP upgrade decisions are separate from the cluster `NodeImage` and `SecurityPatch` channels. - We recommend using a maintenance window of four hours or more for reliable operation.-- If no maintenance configuration exists, AKS might use a fallback schedule to pick up new images, which can cause images to be picked up at unexpected times. You can avoid unexpected timing of new images and upgrades by defining an explicit `aksManagedNodeOSUpgradeSchedule`.+- If the provider doesn't find upcoming maintenance-window data, it treats the window as open. Routine image roll-forward can therefore happen outside an explicitly configured window. - Allow at least 30 minutes between creating or updating a maintenance configuration and the scheduled start time to ensure AKS has time to reconcile the new configuration.  ### Recommended schedule pattern for NAP-managed nodes@@ -27,84 +42,12 @@ We recommend the following schedule pattern for NAP-managed nodes:  - **Weekly cadence**: Recommended for routine node image roll outs (for example: *Every week on Sunday*). -## Create a node OS maintenance schedule example--The following sections show you how to create a weekly maintenance window for NAP-managed nodes using the Azure CLI and a JSON configuration file and how to update, view, list, and delete the maintenance configuration.--### Create a maintenance configuration--1. This status code helps clients understand the purpose of the redirect. Application Gateway for Containers supports the following status codes in the `statusCode` field of the RequestRedirect filter: -- 301 (Moved permanently): Indicates that the target resource is assigned a new permanent URI. Any future references to this resource use one of the enclosed URIs. Use 301 for HTTP to HTTPS redirection of browser traffic.+- **302 (Found):** The target resource is temporarily under a different URI. Since the redirection can change, the client should continue to use the effective request URI for future requests.+- **303 (See Other):** The target resource redirects the user agent to a different resource, as indicated by a URI in the `Location` header field.+- **307 (Temporary Redirect):** The resource is temporarily available at another URI. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the request method and body. Future requests should continue using the original URI.+- **308 (Permanent Redirect):** The resource has a new permanent URI. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the request method and body. Future requests should use the new URI.++Tip++Many clients rewrite a POST to a GET when they follow a 301 or 302 redirect, and the request body is dropped. Confirm the pending or replacement pod schedules on an eligible node in a permitted topology domain. Eligible domains depend on topology labels, selectors or affinity, and the configured node inclusion policies.++When there are fewer eligible domains than `minDomains`, the global minimum becomes zero. Restore sufficient genuinely eligible domains or correct an unintended restriction.+2. Change skew or domain requirements only after assessing availability intent. `ScheduleAnyway` makes the policy soft; successful placement after that change doesn't prove the original hard requirement is met.+3. Inspect the claim's events and class.++    ```bash+    kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace>+    kubectl get pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get storageclass <storageclass-name> -o yaml+    ```+2. Verify the provisioner is available and inspect its controllers and events. Resolve the actual authorization, SKU, capacity, or binding error rather than scaling CPU nodes blindly.+3. For new topology-aware Azure Disk claims, choose an appropriate working class by using `WaitForFirstConsumer`.+4. Preserve existing data and reclaim-policy semantics. Before replacing an unbound claim, verify that it has no data to preserve and that replacement is appropriate. Don't delete production claims as a generic binding remedy.+5. Confirm binding, pod scheduling, successful mounting, and a real data-access check.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes exceed max volume count++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes exceed max volume count.++### Cause++The pod's distinct CSI volumes, together with volumes already needed on the node, exceed the driver's advertised per-node attachment count. This condition isn't a disk-size limit or a CPU shortage.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the maximum volume count issue:++1. Inspect the real driver limit and claims:++    ```bash+    kubectl get csinode <eligible-node> -o yaml+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>+    ```+2. For Azure Disks, examine `disk.csi.azure.com` under `CSINode.spec.drivers`, including `allocatable.count`. Compare volume demand from this and other assigned pods.+3. Place the workload on an eligible node size with sufficient real attachment capacity, distribute workloads appropriately, or use a storage design suitable for the required volume count.+4. Keep storage topology and access modes compatible. Fewer GiB per disk don't reduce the number of attachments.+5. Confirm every required volume mounts and supports real data access. Don't patch CSI limits or fabricate volume handles. See [Azure Disk per-node volume guidance](/en-us/azure/aks/azure-disks-dynamic-pv).++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports.++### Cause++Another assigned pod reserves an overlapping `hostPort` on eligible nodes. The scheduler checks requested host IP, protocol, and port; a CPU-capacity increase on the same node doesn't release that reservation.++This error isn't a Service `NodePort` allocation error. A host process causing a bind failure after placement is also a different diagnostic path.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the unavailable host-port issue:++1. Inspect declared ports and assigned pods.++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<eligible-node> -o yaml+    ```+2. Release only an obsolete authorized reservation, choose a nonconflicting port, or provide another eligible node.+3. If the workload doesn't need direct host-port binding, use an appropriate Service design instead.+4. Confirm scheduling and the application's intended network behavior. Successful scheduling alone doesn't confirm that an application is listening.+ ## References  - [Kubernetes: Use Azure Disks with Azure Kubernetes Service](/en-us/azure/aks/azure-disks-dynamic-pv) - [Kubernetes: Use node taints](/en-us/azure/aks/use-node-taints) - [Kubernetes Documentation: Insufficient CPU](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/resource-bin-packing/#insufficient-resource)-- [Kubernetes Documentation: Assign and Schedule Pods with Taints and Tolerations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/)+- [Managed AKS GPU node guidance](/en-us/azure/aks/aks-managed-gpu-nodes)+- [AKS GPU autoscaling example](/en-us/azure/aks/autoscale-gpu-workloads-with-keda)  **Third-party contact disclaimer**

Implicit snapshot selection isn't supported.+- Restore requires a Ready, non-cordoned virtual node with the snapshot's sandbox-group identifier. The node must satisfy the pod's selectors, required node affinity, and taint tolerations. Don't change sandbox-group labels to bypass placement checks.+- Incomplete init containers, native sidecars with `restartPolicy: Always`, and ephemeral containers aren't supported. One-shot init containers must complete successfully before capture.+- Container identity must match the selected snapshot, including container names, images, commands, and arguments. Create a raw Pod or use the Agent Sandbox restore workflow instead.+- Snapshots capture one pod's runtime state. They aren't application-consistent backups of a distributed service or replacements for persistent-volume backups. Validate external network sessions, remote leases, and external service state after restore.+- Restore requires the custom Kubernetes `restore` permission on the selected snapshot, in addition to permission to create the workload. For Sandbox workloads, authorize the controller that creates the pod; granting it restore permission delegates that access to users who can make it create restore pods.+- Keep Pod snapshot and the serverless runtime running until snapshot deletion completes. Cleanup requires a Ready virtual node with the recorded sandbox-group identifier. Don't remove finalizers to bypass failed cleanup.+- AKS Automatic isn't yet supported.++## How snapshot and restore work++The extension uses the following Kubernetes resources:++| Resource | Purpose |+| --- | --- |+| **PodSnapshotStorageConfig** | Selects the managed VN2 snapshot storage backend. This resource is cluster-scoped. |+| **PodSnapshotPolicy** | Selects eligible pods and defines capture and retention behavior in a namespace. |+| **PodSnapshotManualTrigger** | Requests a capture of a specific pod under a named policy. |+| **PodSnapshot** | Records the resulting snapshot, its source identity, provider storage details, and readiness. |++For the Serverless sandbox runtime powered by ACI, the runtime-provided VN2 snapshot agent captures the sandbox state and records the result through the Pod snapshot extension. ACI manages snapshot storage. You don't configure Azure Blob storage or broker workload identity for this runtime.++On restore, specify a snapshot explicitly. Admission resolves the snapshot, authorizes the caller, validates the workload, and selects a Ready virtual node that has the snapshot's sandbox-group identifier and satisfies the pod's scheduling constraints. It injects the provider restore annotation so the runtime can restore the captured state. Restore doesn't require Blob downloads or node-local staging. If authorization, compatibility, or node-selection checks fail, the request is rejected rather than silently starting a fresh workload.++Warning++Snapshots contain captured workload state, which can include credentials and other sensitive data in memory. ACI manages snapshot storage; you don't configure a customer storage account for this backend. Restrict snapshot restore permissions and access to workloads that can request restore. Don't inject runtime-private restore annotations or disable the restore admission guards.++## Prepare the Workload Manager environment++The following steps create billable Azure resources. Use a dedicated resource group and keep the deployment values unchanged throughout provisioning.++1. Install or update the Workload Manager CLI extension to preview version `1.0.0b1`.++    ```powershell+    az extension add --name workload-manager --version 1.0.0b1 `+      --allow-preview true --upgrade+    ```++    Verify the installed version.++    ```powershell+    az extension show --name workload-manager --query version --output tsv+    ```+2. Set your subscription ID, resource group name, and workload space name. The workload space name must contain 3 to 16 lowercase letters or digits.++    ```powershell+    $SUBSCRIPTION_ID = "<subscription-id>"+    $RESOURCE_GROUP = "<new-resource-group-name>"+    $SPACE_NAME = "<workload-space-name>"+    $LOCATION = "<supported-region>"+    $SUBSCRIPTION_SCOPE = "/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID"+    $RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE = "$SUBSCRIPTION_SCOPE/resourceGroups/$RESOURCE_GROUP"+    $WORKLOAD_SPACE_ID = "$RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE/providers/Microsoft.Compute/workloadSpaces/$SPACE_NAME"+    $AKS_BINDING_NAME = "$SPACE_NAME-aks"+    $ACI_BINDING_NAME = "$SPACE_NAME-aci"+    $LINK_NAME = "$SPACE_NAME-link"+    $AKS_BINDING_ID = "$WORKLOAD_SPACE_ID/runtimeBindings/$AKS_BINDING_NAME"+    $ACI_BINDING_ID = "$WORKLOAD_SPACE_ID/runtimeBindings/$ACI_BINDING_NAME"+    ```+3. Register and select a regional ARM cloud profile. This profile routes ARM requests to `https://westcentralus.management.azure.com/`. Azure CLI discovers the other endpoints automatically. If the profile is already registered, skip the registration command and select it.++    ```powershell+    az cloud register `+      --name WorkloadRP-WestCentralUS `+      --endpoint-resource-manager "https://westcentralus.management.azure.com/"+    ```++    ```powershell+    az cloud set --name WorkloadRP-WestCentralUS+    ```+4. Sign in to the selected cloud and set your subscription before registering features, assigning roles, or creating resources. Sign in again after changing cloud profiles; an existing AzureCloud session doesn't replace this step.++    The `--subscription` option for `az login` requires Azure CLI 2.85.0 or later, as specified in the prerequisites.++    ```powershell+    az login --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID"+    ```+5. Register the preview feature if it isn't already registered, and check its registration status.++    ```powershell+    az feature register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name WorkloadManagerPreview+    ```++    ```powershell+    az feature show --namespace Microsoft.Compute `+      --name WorkloadManagerPreview --query properties.state --output tsv+    ```++    Repeat the `show` command until it returns `Registered`. Don't continue until registration is complete.+6. Create the resource group for the workload space and its managed resources.++    ```powershell+    az group create --name "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --location westcentralus+    ```+7. Register the required resource providers.++    ```powershell+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --wait+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerService --wait+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerInstance --wait+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Network --wait+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ManagedIdentity --wait+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.KubernetesConfiguration --wait+    ```++## Authorize the Workload Manager application++A subscription administrator must grant the Workload Manager application (`032854b2-ba65-4dd6-bdd4-4e86b8756667`) the following roles at the resource group scope. Azure CLI resolves the application to its service principal in the tenant you're signed in to.++Before assigning permissions to either application in this procedure, record any existing role assignments. For each newly created assignment, save the `id` returned by Azure CLI for cleanup. An existing assignment isn't a walkthrough-created resource and must not be removed during cleanup.++A repeated create command can return an existing assignment. Don't treat its returned ID as a newly created assignment.++The `--assignee` option requires a Microsoft Graph lookup. If token-protection Conditional Access blocks Microsoft Graph authentication, ask a directory administrator for each application's tenant-specific service principal **Object ID** from **Enterprise applications** in the Microsoft Entra admin center. This isn't the application ID shown above. Use `--assignee-object-id` together with `--assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal` to avoid the Graph lookup without changing the required Azure permissions.++For example, use the following alternative for the Workload Manager Contributor grant. Use the same two assignee options for its other grants, preserving each role, scope, and condition.++```powershell+az role assignment create `+  --assignee-object-id "<workload-manager-service-principal-object-id>" `+  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `+  --role "Contributor" `+  --scope "$RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE"+```++| Role | Purpose |+| --- | --- |+| **Contributor** | Creates and manages the Azure infrastructure. |+| **Role Based Access Control Administrator** | Creates and deletes role assignments, subject to the condition below. |+| **Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin** | Configures Kubernetes resources on the managed cluster. |++1. Grant **Contributor** and **Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin** at the resource group scope.++    ```powershell+    az role assignment create `+      --assignee "032854b2-ba65-4dd6-bdd4-4e86b8756667" `+      --role "Contributor" `+      --scope "$RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE"++    az role assignment create `+      --assignee "032854b2-ba65-4dd6-bdd4-4e86b8756667" `+      --role "Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin" `+      --scope "$RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE"+    ```+2. Define a condition that restricts write and delete operations on role assignments to service principals, including managed identities, and to these roles: Contributor, Network Contributor, and Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster Admin Role.++    Normalize the condition to a single line before passing it to Azure CLI.++    ```powershell+    $ROLE_CONDITION = @'+    (+      !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write'})+      OR (+        @Request[Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments:RoleDefinitionId] ForAnyOfAnyValues:GuidEquals {b24988ac-6180-42a0-ab88-20f7382dd24c, 4d97b98b-1d4f-4787-a291-c67834d212e7, 0ab0b1a8-8aac-4efd-b8c2-3ee1fb270be8}+        AND @Request[Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments:PrincipalType] ForAnyOfAnyValues:StringEqualsIgnoreCase {'ServicePrincipal'}+      )+    ) AND (+      !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete'})+      OR (+        @Resource[Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments:RoleDefinitionId] ForAnyOfAnyValues:GuidEquals {b24988ac-6180-42a0-ab88-20f7382dd24c, 4d97b98b-1d4f-4787-a291-c67834d212e7, 0ab0b1a8-8aac-4efd-b8c2-3ee1fb270be8}+        AND @Resource[Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments:PrincipalType] ForAnyOfAnyValues:StringEqualsIgnoreCase {'ServicePrincipal'}+      )+    )+    '@+    $ROLE_CONDITION = ($ROLE_CONDITION -replace '[\r\n]+', ' ').Trim()+    ```+3. Assign **Role Based Access Control Administrator** with that condition.++    ```powershell+    az role assignment create `+      --assignee "032854b2-ba65-4dd6-bdd4-4e86b8756667" `+      --role "Role Based Access Control Administrator" `+      --scope "$RESOURCE_GROUP_SCOPE" `+      --condition "$ROLE_CONDITION" `+      --condition-version 2.0+    ```++    The condition limits this role assignment only. It doesn't restrict permissions granted through other assignments.++## Authorize the Compute Sandbox Groups application++For this preview, grant the **Compute Sandbox Groups** service principal (application ID `1eeacc2b-ec4a-4b1e-977a-2b5fef2131c6`) the **Contributor**, **Azure Deployment Stack Owner**, and **Storage Blob Data Contributor** roles at the subscription scope. The resource-group condition assigned to Workload Manager doesn't limit this application's access.++1. As an authorized administrator, assign the three roles.++    ```powershell+    $SANDBOX_ROLES = @(+      "Contributor"+      "Azure Deployment Stack Owner"+      "Storage Blob Data Contributor"+    )++    foreach ($ROLE in $SANDBOX_ROLES) {+      az role assignment create `+        --assignee "1eeacc2b-ec4a-4b1e-977a-2b5fef2131c6" `+        --role "$ROLE" `+        --scope "$SUBSCRIPTION_SCOPE"+    }+    ```++    If Microsoft Graph authentication is blocked, replace the `az role assignment create` command inside the loop with this alternative. Use the Compute Sandbox Groups service principal's tenant-specific Object ID, not its application ID.++    ```powershell+    az role assignment create `+      --assignee-object-id "<compute-sandbox-groups-service-principal-object-id>" `+      --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `+      --role "$ROLE" `+      --scope "$SUBSCRIPTION_SCOPE"+    ```+2. Allow time for both applications' role assignments to propagate before creating the workload space and runtimes.++## Create the workload space and bindings++Create the resources in the following order. Provisioning the AKS and ACI bindings can take several minutes. For each binding and link, repeat its `show` command until `provisioningState` is `Succeeded` before continuing. Each binding must also have a nonempty `providerResourceId`.++The Workload Manager CLI extension version `1.0.0b1` doesn't expose a separate readiness `state` in its `show` output. Provisioning success alone doesn't verify that Pod snapshot is installed or ready to capture and restore workloads. Complete the extension and controller checks in the following list before deploying workloads.++1. Create the workload space, which manages the lifecycle of the runtime composition.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space create `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --location "$LOCATION"+    ```++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$SPACE_NAME"+    ```++    Wait for the parent resource's `provisioningState` to be `Succeeded` before creating the bindings.+2. Create the managed AKS binding with the `Standard` offering.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding create `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$AKS_BINDING_NAME" `+      --location "$LOCATION" `+      --kind Kubernetes `+      --managed '{managed-profile:{offering:Standard}}'+    ```++    Check the AKS binding.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$AKS_BINDING_NAME"+    ```+3. Create the managed ACI binding for the serverless sandbox runtime.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding create `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$ACI_BINDING_NAME" `+      --location "$LOCATION" `+      --kind ServerlessContainers `+      --managed '{managed-profile:{provider:ACI}}'+    ```++    Check the ACI binding.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$ACI_BINDING_NAME"+    ```+4. Check the underlying AKS and ACI resources before creating the runtime link. A binding can report `Succeeded` before its provider resource is ready.++    ```powershell+    foreach ($BINDING_NAME in @($AKS_BINDING_NAME, $ACI_BINDING_NAME)) {+      $PROVIDER_RESOURCE_ID = az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding show `+        --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+        --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+        --name "$BINDING_NAME" `+        --query properties.providerResourceId --output tsv++      if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or+          [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($PROVIDER_RESOURCE_ID)) {+        throw "Couldn't resolve the provider resource for $BINDING_NAME."+      }++      az resource show --ids "$PROVIDER_RESOURCE_ID" `+        --query '{name:name,state:properties.provisioningState}'+    }+    ```++    Repeat the checks until both resources report `Succeeded`. If either resource reports `Failed`, resolve its provisioning error before continuing.+5. Link the AKS orchestrator to the serverless sandbox runtime by using the bindings' full resource IDs.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-link create `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$LINK_NAME" `+      --location "$LOCATION" `+      --orchestrator-binding "$AKS_BINDING_ID" `+      --execution-binding "$ACI_BINDING_ID"+    ```++    If creation returns `ProviderNotReady`, repeat the provider-resource checks, allow time for readiness to propagate, and retry the same create command. Don't recreate the workload space or bindings. Check that the runtime link reaches `Succeeded` before installing Pod snapshot.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space runtime-link show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$LINK_NAME"+    ```+6. Resolve the managed AKS cluster on which you'll install the Pod snapshot extension.++    ```powershell+    $AKS_RESOURCE_ID = az workload-manager workload-space runtime-binding show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --space-name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --name "$AKS_BINDING_NAME" `+      --query properties.providerResourceId `+      --output tsv++    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($AKS_RESOURCE_ID)) {+      throw "The AKS binding didn't return a providerResourceId. Wait for provisioning to complete and try again."+    }+    ```++    ```powershell+    $AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS = $AKS_RESOURCE_ID.Trim('/').Split('/')+    if ($AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS.Length -ne 8 -or+        $AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS[2] -ne 'resourceGroups' -or+        $AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS[5] -ne 'Microsoft.ContainerService' -or+        $AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS[6] -ne 'managedClusters') {+      throw "The AKS binding didn't return a managed cluster resource ID."+    }++    $AKS_CLUSTER = az aks show `+      --resource-group "$($AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS[3])" `+      --name "$($AKS_RESOURCE_PARTS[7])" `+      --query '{name:name,resourceGroup:resourceGroup,kubernetesVersion:kubernetesVersion}' `+      --output json | ConvertFrom-Json++    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or $null -eq $AKS_CLUSTER) {+      throw "Couldn't read the managed AKS cluster. Check binding provisioning and your access."+    }++    $CLUSTER_NAME = $AKS_CLUSTER.name+    $AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP = $AKS_CLUSTER.resourceGroup+    $AKS_CLUSTER+    ```++    Confirm that `kubernetesVersion` is 1.35 or later. Keep `RESOURCE_GROUP` unchanged: it identifies the workload space's resource group, which can differ from `AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP`.+7. Grant the walkthrough user Kubernetes administrator access if they don't already have it. Workload Manager's application role assignments don't grant your account access to Kubernetes resources. For a cluster that uses Azure RBAC, an authorized administrator can assign **Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin** at the cluster scope. These commands assign the role to the signed-in user.++    If Microsoft Graph authentication is blocked, replace the `az ad signed-in-user show` assignment with `$USER_OBJECT_ID = "<user-object-id>"`, using the user Object ID supplied by your directory administrator.++    ```powershell+    $USER_OBJECT_ID = az ad signed-in-user show --query id --output tsv+    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or+        [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($USER_OBJECT_ID)) {+      throw "Couldn't resolve the signed-in user."+    }++    az role assignment create `+      --assignee-object-id "$USER_OBJECT_ID" `+      --assignee-principal-type User `+      --role "Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin" `+      --scope "$AKS_RESOURCE_ID"+    ```++    Record the assignment ID if you create it for this walkthrough. Allow time for role propagation before running Kubernetes commands. Getting cluster credentials alone doesn't grant Kubernetes access.++## Install the Pod snapshot cluster extension++Install the extension directly on the managed AKS cluster by using `az k8s-extension` with the cluster name and resource group resolved from the AKS runtime binding. Run these commands in the same PowerShell session as the setup steps.++Use Pod snapshot extension version `0.1.1` or later. The create command doesn't pin a version and uses the service-offered version with automatic upgrades enabled by default.++You can install Pod snapshot and Agent Sandbox in either order. The Pod snapshot manager detects the Sandbox API when it becomes available, including after the manager starts, without requiring a restart. Agent Sandbox isn't required to capture and restore raw Pods.++1. Install or update the cluster extension CLI.++    ```powershell+    az extension add --name k8s-extension --upgrade+    ```+2. Create the Pod snapshot extension for the serverless sandbox runtime.++    ```powershell+    az k8s-extension create `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --cluster-type managedClusters `+      --name pod-snapshot `+      --extension-type Microsoft.PodSnapshot `+      --configuration-settings `+        "nodeWorker.enabled=false" `+        "broker.enabled=false"+    ```++    These settings disable the node worker and Azure Blob access broker. The serverless runtime provides its own snapshot agent and managed storage; don't configure Blob storage or broker workload identity for this installation.+3. Check the extension's provisioning state and installed version.++    ```powershell+    az k8s-extension show `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --cluster-type managedClusters `+      --name pod-snapshot `+      --query '{type:extensionType,state:provisioningState,version:currentVersion}'+    ```++    Continue only after `state` is `Succeeded` and `version` is `0.1.1` or later. A successful installation of an older version doesn't meet this requirement.+4. Check the workload space again after you provision its bindings and runtime link and install Pod snapshot.++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space show `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --query 'properties.{provisioningState:provisioningState}'+    ```++    Continue only after `provisioningState` is `Succeeded`. This CLI check doesn't verify aggregate readiness or workload behavior. Complete the Kubernetes checks in the next step.+5. Connect to the managed AKS cluster and wait for the Pod snapshot manager to become Ready before applying snapshot resources.++    ```powershell+    $KUBE_CONTEXT = "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID-$SPACE_NAME"+    az aks get-credentials `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --context "$KUBE_CONTEXT" `+      --overwrite-existing++    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {+      throw "Couldn't get cluster credentials. Check the cluster and your access before continuing."+    }++    kubectl config use-context "$KUBE_CONTEXT"+    ```++    Configure Kubernetes authentication to use your current Azure CLI sign-in instead of starting a separate device-code sign-in.++    ```powershell+    kubelogin convert-kubeconfig --login azurecli+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n pod-snapshot-system rollout status `+      deployment/pod-snapshot-manager --timeout=10m+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n pod-snapshot-system get pods -o wide+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl get runtimeclass virtualnode2 -o yaml+    ```++    Continue only after the manager rollout succeeds and the `virtualnode2` RuntimeClass exists. If a check fails, resolve the installation or runtime configuration before creating snapshot resources.++## Configure a storage resource and policy++Create a cluster-scoped storage configuration that selects the managed VN2 backend. This Pod snapshot storage configuration doesn't require a customer storage account, container, Blob role assignment, or broker workload identity. The runtime manages snapshot storage.++1. Create `vn2-storage.yaml` with the following content. Don't specify a namespace because `PodSnapshotStorageConfig` is cluster-scoped.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/v1alpha1+    kind: PodSnapshotStorageConfig+    metadata:+      name: vn2-storage+    spec:+      snapshotStorageConfig:+        managedVn2: {}+    ```+2. Apply the storage configuration and inspect it.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f vn2-storage.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl get podsnapshotstorageconfig vn2-storage -o yaml+    ```++Use the managed VN2 storage configuration for the serverless workload. The ACI runtime manages snapshot execution and storage.++1. Verify the runtime and virtual node.++    ```powershell+    kubectl get runtimeclass virtualnode2 -o yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl get nodes `+      -L podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/sandbox-group-identifier+    ```++    Continue only when the runtime exists and its virtual node is Ready with a nonempty sandbox-group identifier. The runtime must provide its snapshot agent and the agent's Kubernetes permissions. Installing Pod snapshot doesn't deploy the VN2 snapshot agent. Don't add or change sandbox-group labels manually.+2. Create `aci-snapshot-policy.yaml`.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: v1+    kind: Namespace+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload-demo+    ---+    apiVersion: podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/v1alpha1+    kind: PodSnapshotPolicy+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload-policy+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    spec:+      storageConfigName: vn2-storage+      selector:+        matchLabels:+          app: aci-workload+      triggerConfig:+        type: manual+        postCheckpoint: resume+    ```++    `postCheckpoint: resume` keeps the source workload running after capture.+3. Apply the policy and wait for it to become Ready.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-snapshot-policy.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready `+      podsnapshotpolicy/aci-workload-policy --timeout=5m+    ```++    If validation fails, inspect the policy's `PolicySpecSupported` and `StorageConfigValid` conditions.++## Prepare your workload++Use a digest-pinned container image that the serverless runtime supports and can pull. Configure image pull credentials if required, and use the same immutable image reference for capture and restore. Your workload doesn't need a specific HTTP endpoint to use Pod snapshot.++Choose a workload with observable application state, such as an in-memory session identifier, initialized application data, or task progress. Adapt the resource settings, commands, arguments, configuration, and health checks to your application. Without an application-specific readiness probe, Pod readiness doesn't establish that initialization has completed.++1. Create `aci-workload.yaml`. Replace `<your-container-image>@sha256:<image-digest>` with your workload image reference and add its application-specific settings. This pod uses `virtualnode2`.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: v1+    kind: Pod+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+      labels:+        app: aci-workload+    spec:+      enableServiceLinks: false+      runtimeClassName: virtualnode2+      containers:+        - name: workload+          image: <your-container-image>@sha256:<image-digest>+          resources:+            requests:+              cpu: "1"+              memory: 1Gi+            limits:+              cpu: "1"+              memory: 1Gi+    ```+2. Apply the manifest and wait for the source pod to become Ready.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-workload.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready `+      pod/aci-workload --timeout=10m+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get pod aci-workload -o wide+    ```++    Verify that the pod runs on the serverless runtime's virtual node before capturing it.+3. Wait for application initialization to finish, then record state that distinguishes a resumed process from a fresh start. Use your application's API, logs, or another application-specific check. Record the expected restored state before creating the trigger. Data read only from an external database or persistent volume doesn't prove that process memory was restored.++## Capture pod state++Capture a Ready pod that matches the policy selector. Don't create a `PodSnapshot` directly; the trigger creates it and records its name.++1. Create `aci-snapshot-trigger.yaml`.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/v1alpha1+    kind: PodSnapshotManualTrigger+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload-snapshot+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    spec:+      targetPod: aci-workload+      policyName: aci-workload-policy+    ```+2. Apply the trigger and wait for completion.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-snapshot-trigger.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Triggered `+      podsnapshotmanualtrigger/aci-workload-snapshot --timeout=10m+    ```+3. Resolve the snapshot name and wait for the snapshot itself to become Ready.++    ```powershell+    $SNAPSHOT_NAME = kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get `+      podsnapshotmanualtrigger aci-workload-snapshot `+      -o jsonpath='{.status.snapshotCreated.name}'++    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($SNAPSHOT_NAME)) {+      throw "The trigger hasn't recorded a snapshot name. Inspect its conditions before continuing."+    }+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready `+      "podsnapshot/$SNAPSHOT_NAME" --timeout=10m+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get podsnapshot "$SNAPSHOT_NAME" -o yaml+    ```++    Confirm that `status.storageStatus.managedVn2` records a nonempty `snapshotName`, a nonempty `sandboxGroupIdentifier`, and a successful `operationState`. This is provider-managed storage, not Azure Blob status. Keep the Kubernetes `PodSnapshot` name in `$SNAPSHOT_NAME`; don't replace it with the provider's `snapshotName`.++## Authorize snapshot restore++The user who creates the restore pod needs permission to create pods and to use the custom `restore` verb on the selected snapshot. The restore label alone doesn't grant access.++Warning++Don't grant the `restore` verb to built-in Kubernetes controllers, such as `system:serviceaccount:kube-system:replicaset-controller` or `system:serviceaccount:kube-system:job-controller`, to enable restore through Deployments, ReplicaSets, or Jobs. The controller creates the Pod, so restore authorization checks the controller's identity, not the user who created the workload. Granting restore access to a controller delegates that access to users who can make it create Pods in the namespace, even if those users don't have restore permission themselves.++1. As a Kubernetes administrator, create `aci-restore-access.yaml`. Replace `<snapshot-name>` with `$SNAPSHOT_NAME` and `<kubernetes-user-name>` with the authenticated Kubernetes username of the user who creates the restore pod.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1+    kind: Role+    metadata:+      name: aci-snapshot-restorer+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    rules:+      - apiGroups: ["podsnapshot.aks.azure.com"]+        resources: ["podsnapshots"]+        resourceNames: ["<snapshot-name>"]+        verbs: ["restore"]+    ---+    apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1+    kind: RoleBinding+    metadata:+      name: aci-user-restorer+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    subjects:+      - kind: User+        name: <kubernetes-user-name>+        apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io+    roleRef:+      kind: Role+      name: aci-snapshot-restorer+      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io+    ```+2. Apply the permissions.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-restore-access.yaml+    ```+3. As the user who will create the restore pod, verify restore permission.++    ```powershell+    kubectl auth can-i restore `+      "podsnapshots.podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/$SNAPSHOT_NAME" `+      --namespace aci-workload-demo+    ```++    The warning `Warning: verb 'restore' is not a known verb` is expected because `restore` is a custom verb. It doesn't indicate an authorization failure. Continue only if the command returns `yes`.++## Start a workload from captured pod state++ACI supports only explicit restore. Specify the name of a Ready snapshot in the same namespace. Admission selects a Ready virtual node with the snapshot's sandbox-group identifier and injects the provider restore annotation.++1. After verifying snapshot readiness, delete the source pod. Keep the policy, storage configuration, snapshot, and serverless runtime.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete pod aci-workload --wait=true+    ```+2. Create `aci-workload-restore.yaml`. Replace `<snapshot-name>` with `$SNAPSHOT_NAME` and use the exact image reference from the source pod. Keep its container name, command, arguments, resource sizing, and `enableServiceLinks` setting unchanged.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: v1+    kind: Pod+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload-restore+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+      labels:+        app: aci-workload+        podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/restore: "true"+      annotations:+        podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/restore-from: <snapshot-name>+    spec:+      enableServiceLinks: false+      runtimeClassName: virtualnode2+      containers:+        - name: workload+          image: <your-container-image>@sha256:<image-digest>+          resources:+            requests:+              cpu: "1"+              memory: 1Gi+            limits:+              cpu: "1"+              memory: 1Gi+    ```++    Copy any application-specific commands, arguments, configuration, health checks, and image pull credentials from your source manifest into the restore manifest. Don't set the internal provider snapshot annotation yourself. If no eligible Ready node matches the snapshot's sandbox group and the pod's scheduling constraints, admission denies the restore instead of starting a new workload.+3. Apply the restore manifest and wait for readiness.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-workload-restore.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready `+      pod/aci-workload-restore --timeout=10m+    ```+4. Use the same application-specific check to compare the restored state with the state recorded before capture. Confirm that initialized data, session identity, or task progress resumed from the captured point rather than returning to its initial state. Check external connections and dependencies separately. A Ready pod or a shorter startup time alone doesn't prove that process state was restored.+5. Inspect the pod's placement and restore event.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get pod aci-workload-restore -o wide+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get events `+      --field-selector involvedObject.name=aci-workload-restore `+      --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'+    ```++    The manager emits `AKSPodRestored` and updates the snapshot's `lastAccessTime` after the restored ACI pod is Ready. Verify application-state continuity as well as the event.++## Restore an Agent Sandbox workload++This section is optional. To install Agent Sandbox version `1.0.7` or later, follow the serverless runtime instructions in the [Agent Sandbox cluster extension](agent-sandbox-cluster-extension) article, and wait for its controller to become Ready. Reuse this workload space and its deployment values. Don't create another workload space, new bindings, or a new runtime link.++You can install Agent Sandbox before or after installing Pod snapshot without restarting the Pod snapshot manager. This example reuses the Ready snapshot and the `aci-snapshot-restorer` Role created earlier. ACI supports only explicit snapshot selection for Pods and Sandbox workloads.++1. As a Kubernetes administrator, create `aci-sandbox-restore-access.yaml` to authorize the Agent Sandbox controller.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1+    kind: RoleBinding+    metadata:+      name: aci-sandbox-restorer+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    subjects:+      - kind: ServiceAccount+        name: agent-sandbox-controller+        namespace: agent-sandbox-system+    roleRef:+      kind: Role+      name: aci-snapshot-restorer+      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-sandbox-restore-access.yaml+    ```++    This binding delegates snapshot restore to users who can make the controller create restore pods. Restrict Sandbox creation and update permissions accordingly.+2. Create `aci-workload-sandbox-restore.yaml`. Replace `<snapshot-name>` with `$SNAPSHOT_NAME` and use the exact image reference from the source pod. Put restore intent on the pod template, not only on Sandbox metadata.++    ```yaml+    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1+    kind: Sandbox+    metadata:+      name: aci-workload-sandbox-restore+      namespace: aci-workload-demo+    spec:+      podTemplate:+        metadata:+          labels:+            app: aci-workload+            example: aci-workload-sandbox-restore+            podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/restore: "true"+          annotations:+            podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/restore-from: <snapshot-name>+        spec:+          enableServiceLinks: false+          runtimeClassName: virtualnode2+          containers:+            - name: workload+              image: <your-container-image>@sha256:<image-digest>+              resources:+                requests:+                  cpu: "1"+                  memory: 1Gi+                limits:+                  cpu: "1"+                  memory: 1Gi+    ```++    Copy your source workload's application-specific commands, arguments, configuration, health checks, and image pull credentials into `spec.podTemplate.spec`. Keep container identity and resource sizing compatible with the snapshot.+3. Apply the manifest and wait for the Sandbox and its backing pod to become Ready.++    ```powershell+    kubectl apply -f aci-workload-sandbox-restore.yaml+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready `+      sandbox/aci-workload-sandbox-restore --timeout=10m+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=condition=Ready pod `+      --selector example=aci-workload-sandbox-restore --timeout=10m+    ```+4. Get the name of the pod created by the Sandbox controller.++    ```powershell+    $ACI_SANDBOX_POD = kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get pods `+      --selector example=aci-workload-sandbox-restore `+      -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'++    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get pod "$ACI_SANDBOX_POD" -o wide+    ```++    Use your application's API, logs, or another application-specific check against this pod to verify the captured state, independently of the earlier raw Pod restore. A Ready Sandbox alone doesn't prove application-state continuity.++## Schedule snapshots and configure retention++This section is optional and doesn't require Agent Sandbox. It reuses the managed VN2 storage configuration and namespace created earlier. Keep at least one eligible workload pod running before you apply the policy.++A cron policy captures one representative Ready pod matching its selector per run, not every matching pod. Use `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` to prevent overlapping captures and `postCheckpoint: resume` to keep the source running. A cron policy with `postCheckpoint: stop` doesn't become Ready.++Create `aci-workload-cron-policy.yaml`:++```yaml+apiVersion: podsnapshot.aks.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: PodSnapshotPolicy+metadata:+  name: aci-workload-nightly+  namespace: aci-workload-demo+spec:+  storageConfigName: vn2-storage+  selector:+    matchLabels:+      app: aci-workload+  triggerConfig:+    type: cron+    schedule: "0 3 * * *"+    timeZone: America/Los_Angeles+    startingDeadlineSeconds: 600+    concurrencyPolicy: Forbid+    postCheckpoint: resume+  retentionConfig:+    maxSnapshots: 7+    lastAccessTimeout: 168h+```++This policy schedules a daily capture at 03:00 in the specified time zone. `startingDeadlineSeconds` limits how late a missed run can start. `maxSnapshots` caps usable Ready snapshots per policy, not per source pod. `lastAccessTimeout` enables cleanup based on the time since a snapshot was last accessed. Protected snapshots can delay retention cleanup while a restore is in flight. Plan for the capacity and cost of provider-managed snapshots, including snapshots retained during protected restores.++```powershell+kubectl apply -f aci-workload-cron-policy.yaml+```++```powershell+kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get podsnapshotpolicy aci-workload-nightly -o yaml+```++ACI supports only explicit restore, including for scheduled snapshots. To restore a scheduled snapshot, specify its name in `restore-from` and update the example Role's `resourceNames` to authorize that exact snapshot. Retention can delete an older snapshot named by the Role. The Role doesn't prevent snapshot deletion.++To stop future scheduled captures, delete the cron policy. The policy doesn't own the snapshots it creates, so deleting the policy preserves them and stops its retention rules from applying to them. Delete those snapshots explicitly when you no longer need them.++## Clean up resources++Stop scheduled captures, delete workload consumers, and then delete snapshots before uninstalling Pod snapshot or deleting the runtime link and bindings. The extension requires the runtime's snapshot agent to complete provider-managed snapshot deletion. If a cleanup command fails or times out, resolve the failure before continuing. Don't remove finalizers to force cleanup.++Run these commands in the same PowerShell session and Kubernetes context used for setup. If you return in a new shell, restore the deployment values and reconnect to the managed AKS cluster first. Set `$SNAPSHOT_NAME` again before running commands that use it. List the snapshots, then replace `<snapshot-name>` with the name of your example snapshot.++```powershell+kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get podsnapshots+$SNAPSHOT_NAME = "<snapshot-name>"+```++Before removing Azure resources or permissions, identify which resources and role assignments you created solely for this walkthrough. Keep the IDs of newly created role assignments so an administrator can remove those exact assignments later. Don't remove preexisting grants or permissions used by other workload spaces.++If you used both articles, stop scheduled captures first, remove Agent Sandbox warm pools and Sandbox consumers in both example namespaces, and then delete snapshots. Complete workload and snapshot cleanup before uninstalling either extension. Uninstall both extensions before deleting the workload space once.++The following commands delete all snapshots in the dedicated `aci-workload-demo` namespace. Don't run them unchanged in a namespace that contains workloads or snapshots you need to keep.++1. If you created the cron policy, delete it first to stop new scheduled captures and wait for its active run to finish. Allow any in-flight manual capture to finish before deleting its trigger or source pod.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete podsnapshotpolicy aci-workload-nightly `+      --ignore-not-found --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```+2. If you created the optional Sandbox, delete it while its controller is running.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete sandbox aci-workload-sandbox-restore `+      --ignore-not-found --cascade=foreground --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```++    Then delete the example pods.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete pod aci-workload aci-workload-restore `+      --ignore-not-found --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```++    Confirm that no example pods remain before deleting snapshots.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get pods+    ```++    If example pods are still terminating, wait for their deletion before continuing. If a pod isn't terminating, investigate its owner and delete the example workload that owns it. If waiting times out, inspect namespace events and controller logs, resolve the reported error, and retry. Keep both controllers and the runtime running; don't force-delete pods or remove finalizers.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo wait --for=delete pods --all --timeout=10m+    ```+3. Delete the trigger and snapshot. Don't continue until cleanup finishes successfully.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete podsnapshotmanualtrigger `+      aci-workload-snapshot --ignore-not-found --wait=true+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete podsnapshot "$SNAPSHOT_NAME" `+      --ignore-not-found --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```+4. Delete all remaining snapshots in the dedicated example namespace, including snapshots created by the cron policy. Wait for their finalizers to finish provider-managed storage cleanup. Don't delete the namespace or runtime resources until all snapshots are deleted.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete podsnapshots --all --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```+5. Confirm that no snapshots remain in the example namespace, then delete the dedicated example namespace if it contains no resources you need to keep.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo get podsnapshots+    ```++    Delete the manual capture policy after its triggers and snapshots are gone.++    ```powershell+    kubectl -n aci-workload-demo delete podsnapshotpolicy aci-workload-policy `+      --ignore-not-found --wait=true --timeout=5m+    ```++    ```powershell+    kubectl delete namespace aci-workload-demo --wait=true --timeout=10m+    ```++    Delete the cluster-scoped storage configuration only if no policies in other namespaces reference it. Otherwise, keep the configuration.++    ```powershell+    kubectl delete podsnapshotstorageconfig vn2-storage `+      --ignore-not-found --wait=true --timeout=5m+    ```+6. If no workloads, snapshots, or policies in any namespace need Pod snapshot, uninstall the `pod-snapshot` cluster extension instance.++    ```powershell+    az k8s-extension delete `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --cluster-type managedClusters `+      --name pod-snapshot `+      --yes+    ```++    List the remaining extensions to verify that `pod-snapshot` is removed.++    ```powershell+    az k8s-extension list `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --cluster-type managedClusters `+      --query '[].{name:name,state:provisioningState}' --output table+    ```++    Uninstalling Pod snapshot doesn't delete the workload space, AKS cluster, or ACI runtime. Those resources can continue to incur charges. Delete them separately only when they're dedicated to this example and no longer needed.+7. Delete the workload space and its owned resources only if you created it solely for this walkthrough and no workloads need it.++    If you installed Agent Sandbox, remove its Sandbox workloads and extension by following its serverless runtime [cleanup procedure](agent-sandbox-cluster-extension#clean-up-resources) before deleting the workload space. Workload-space deletion removes its owned AKS and ACI resources and can permanently delete workload data. The resource group and both applications' prerequisite role assignments remain. Don't delete a shared workload space or resource group.++    Record the AKS managed node resource group's name before deleting the workload space.++    ```powershell+    $NODE_RESOURCE_GROUP = az aks show `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --resource-group "$AKS_RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$CLUSTER_NAME" `+      --query nodeResourceGroup --output tsv+    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($NODE_RESOURCE_GROUP)) {+      throw "Couldn't retrieve the AKS managed node resource group."+    }+    ```++    ```powershell+    az workload-manager workload-space delete `+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --name "$SPACE_NAME" `+      --yes+    ```++    Wait for deletion to finish. Verify that the workload space no longer exists and that its owned AKS and ACI resources no longer appear in their resource groups. Investigate any remaining managed resources before considering infrastructure cleanup complete.+8. Switch back to the standard Azure cloud profile when you finish using the regional endpoint. This step doesn't delete any resources.++    ```powershell+    az cloud set --name AzureCloud+    ```+9. Optionally, delete the resource group only if you created it solely for this walkthrough and it contains no resources you need to keep.++    Complete workload and snapshot cleanup first. Keep the prerequisite application grants until infrastructure deletion finishes, including when resource-group deletion is used to recover a failed workload-space deletion.++    Verify that both the dedicated resource group and the managed node resource group are gone before considering cleanup complete.++    ```powershell+    az group delete `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --name "$RESOURCE_GROUP" `+      --yes+    ```++    Verify that the command returns `false`.++    ```powershell+    az group exists `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --name "$RESOURCE_GROUP"+    ```++    Verify that the managed node resource group check also returns `false`.++    ```powershell+    az group exists `+      --subscription "$SUBSCRIPTION_ID" `+      --name "$NODE_RESOURCE_GROUP"+    ```+10. After infrastructure cleanup, have your subscription administrator review the application role assignments created for this walkthrough. Remove an assignment only if it still exists, you created it during this walkthrough, and no other workload space or service needs it. Don't remove preexisting or shared assignments.++    Subscription-scoped grants can be shared across teams' resource groups. Deleting your workload space or resource group doesn't mean those grants are unused.++    Use the assignment's `id` from the corresponding `az role assignment create` output. Repeat for each assignment approved for removal.++    ```powershell+    az role assignment delete `+      --ids "<role-assignment-resource-id-created-for-this-walkthrough>"+    ```++::: zone-end

                                                                                                                            @@ -10,6 +10,29 @@ Starting on **November 30, 2025**, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) no longer supp  `AKSNodeClass` resources enable you to configure Azure-specific settings for NAP. Each [`NodePool` resource](node-auto-provisioning-node-pools) must reference an `AKSNodeClass` using `spec.template.spec.nodeClassRef`. You can have multiple `NodePools` that point to the same `AKSNodeClass`, allowing you to share common Azure configurations across different node pools. +## Kubernetes and node image versions++NAP allows you to control the Kubernetes and node image versions by using the `spec.versions` field in the `AKSNodeClass`. If you omit `spec.versions`, the node Kubernetes version follows the observed AKS control-plane version, and NAP automatically resolves compatible node images. When the control-plane version increases, NAP considers the nodes as `Drifted`, marks images as not ready, and resolves images for the new Kubernetes version. NAP doesn't currently automatically downgrade node Kubernetes versions.++For an up-to-date list of supported Kubernetes versions and node image versions, see the [AKS Release Tracker](https://releases.aks.azure.com/).++### Pin Kubernetes version++Set `spec.versions.kubernetesVersion` to pin the node Kubernetes version. Specify the full `major.minor.patch` version. AKS supports the version, and it's compatible with the control plane: it has the same major version, can't have a higher minor version, and can't be more than three minor versions behind. If the node and control plane use the same minor version, the node patch version can't be higher than the control-plane patch version. An invalid format, incompatible version, or unsupported target keeps the Kubernetes version condition false, so the `AKSNodeClass` isn't ready for provisioning.++### Pin node image version++Set `spec.versions.nodeImageVersion` to pin a node image version suffix. This value is the suffix after `/versions/` in an image ID, not a full image ID or an arbitrary value. The requested suffix must be present in the `AKSNodeClass` status as a currently resolved image, the latest image version, or a recently used image version. A recently used image version must be paired with its recorded Kubernetes version. The Kubernetes version and image version must be specified together: `nodeImageVersion` requires `kubernetesVersion`. If you change the Kubernetes version while pinning a current or latest image version, that combination must also be a recently used Kubernetes and image version pair.++Pinning an image version prevents automatic image roll-forward. To resume automatic image selection, remove `nodeImageVersion`; you can keep `kubernetesVersion` pinned if needed. The following example shows both fields. Replace the values with a supported Kubernetes version and an eligible image version suffix for your `AKSNodeClass`:++```yaml+spec:+  versions:+    kubernetesVersion: "1.34.0"+    nodeImageVersion: "2026.09.23"+```+ Important  Changing a setting on an existing `AKSNodeClass` doesn't reconfigure running nodes in place. NAP marks the nodes provisioned from the previous configuration as *drifted* and replaces them, subject to the disruption controls on the referencing `NodePool` resources. The `tags` field is the only exception, because tag changes apply to existing Azure resources without replacing the node. To learn more, see [Drift](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#drift) and [Disruption budgets](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#disruption-budgets). Before you modify an `AKSNodeClass` that production workloads use, review this guidance.@@ -117,6 +140,41 @@ spec:   fipsMode: FIPS ``` +## Workload runtime and pod sandboxing++NAP supports [pod sandboxing](concepts-pod-sandboxing) on provisioned nodes.
